stem: The energy stored in a charged capacitor is represented by which area?

options.content: The area under a graph of charge (y-axis) against time (x-axis)
options.rationale: This area has units C s, which is not an energy.

options.content: The area under a graph of p.d. (y-axis) against charge (x-axis)
options.rationale: Correct: ΔW = VΔQ for each small charge added.

options.content: The gradient of a graph of charge against p.d.
options.rationale: That gradient is the capacitance.

options.content: The area under a graph of current against time
options.rationale: That area is the charge that has flowed.

explanation: Work to add charge ΔQ at p.d. V is VΔQ, so the energy is the area under the V-Q graph: a triangle, ½QV.

stem: What energy is stored in a $100\ \mu\text{F}$ capacitor charged to $50\ \text{V}$?

options.rationale: This forgets the ½.
This forgets to square V.
Correct: ½CV² = ½ × 100 × 10⁻⁶ × 2500.
This leaves C in µF instead of F.

explanation: $W = \tfrac{1}{2}CV^2 = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 100 \times 10^{-6} \times 50^2 = 0.125\ \text{J}$.

stem: The p.d. across a capacitor is tripled. By what factor does the energy stored change?

options.rationale: The charge triples, but the energy depends on V².
There is no reason for a factor 2 × 3.
Correct: W ∝ V².
This halves the factor of 3 by misusing the ½ in ½CV².

explanation: W = ½CV², so tripling V multiplies W by 3² = 9.

stem: A $47\ \mu\text{F}$ capacitor holds a charge of $3.0\ \text{mC}$. What energy does it store?

options.rationale: This forgets the factor 2 in the denominator.
This multiplies Q by C instead of using V = Q/C.
This is V/2, a p.d., not an energy: Q is not squared.
Correct: Q²/2C.

hints: Use the form with Q and C.

stem: A battery of e.m.f. E charges an uncharged capacitor fully through a resistor. Which statement about the energy is correct?

options.content: The battery supplies ½QE, all of which is stored in the capacitor.
options.rationale: The battery moves all the charge through its full e.m.f., supplying QE.

options.content: A smaller resistor reduces the energy dissipated, so more than half is stored.
options.rationale: A smaller R gives a bigger current for a shorter time; the loss is still ½QE.

options.content: The battery supplies QE and all of it is stored, because the capacitor has no resistance.
options.rationale: Only ½QE is stored; the rest heats the circuit resistance.

options.content: The battery supplies QE; half is stored and half is dissipated in the resistor, whatever its resistance.
options.rationale: Correct: the loss is ½QE independent of R.

explanation: Energy supplied = QE; stored = ½QE; the other ½QE is dissipated in the resistance (and radiated), independent of R.
hints: Charge Q passes through the whole e.m.f. of the battery.

stem: A capacitor in a clock's backup supply discharges until its p.d. has fallen to half its initial value. What fraction of the initial stored energy has been delivered?

options.rationale: Correct: W ∝ V², so ¼ remains and ¾ has been delivered.
Energy is not proportional to V.
This is the fraction remaining, not the fraction delivered.
Energy depends on V², not V³.

explanation: W ∝ V². At half the p.d., (½)² = ¼ of the energy remains, so ¾ has been delivered.
hints: Compare W at V and at V/2.

stem: Calculate the energy stored in a $4700\ \mu\text{F}$ capacitor charged to $9.0\ \text{V}$, in J, to three significant figures.
A defibrillator's $25\ \mu\text{F}$ capacitor must store $150\ \text{J}$. Calculate the p.d. to which it must be charged, in V, to three significant figures.
explanation:
1. $W = \tfrac{1}{2}CV^2$, so $V = \sqrt{\dfrac{2W}{C}}$.
2. $V = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 \times 150}{25 \times 10^{-6}}} = 3.46 \times 10^{3}\ \text{V}$.
3. Forgetting the 2 gives a value about 30% too small.
workedSolution:
1. 1. $W = \tfrac{1}{2}CV^2$, so $V = \sqrt{\dfrac{2W}{C}}$.
2. $V = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 \times 150}{25 \times 10^{-6}}} = 3.46 \times 10^{3}\ \text{V}$.
3. Forgetting the 2 gives a value about 30% too small.

stem: A $1000\ \mu\text{F}$ capacitor charged to $200\ \text{V}$ is discharged through a spot-welding electrode in $2.0\ \text{ms}$. Calculate the average power delivered, in W, to two significant figures.
hints: Find the energy, then divide by the time.

stem: A $10\ \mu\text{F}$ capacitor charged to $12\ \text{V}$ is connected across an uncharged $30\ \mu\text{F}$ capacitor. Calculate the energy dissipated during the sharing of charge, in J, to two significant figures.
explanation:
1. Before: $W_1 = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 10 \times 10^{-6} \times 12^2 = 7.2 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{J}$.
2. Common p.d. $= \dfrac{120\ \mu\text{C}}{40\ \mu\text{F}} = 3\ \text{V}$.
3. After: $W_2 = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 40 \times 10^{-6} \times 3^2 = 1.8 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{J}$.
4. Dissipated $= 5.4 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{J}$ (three quarters of the original energy here). Half is lost only when the capacitors are equal.
workedSolution:
1. 1. Before: $W_1 = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 10 \times 10^{-6} \times 12^2 = 7.2 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{J}$.
2. Common p.d. $= \dfrac{120\ \mu\text{C}}{40\ \mu\text{F}} = 3\ \text{V}$.
3. After: $W_2 = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 40 \times 10^{-6} \times 3^2 = 1.8 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{J}$.
4. Dissipated $= 5.4 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{J}$ (three quarters of the original energy here). Half is lost only when the capacitors are equal.
hints: Charge is conserved, energy is not.

stem: A memory chip draws an average power of $20\ \text{mW}$ from a $2200\ \mu\text{F}$ backup capacitor charged to $5.0\ \text{V}$. The chip stops working when the p.d. falls below $3.0\ \text{V}$. Estimate how long the backup lasts, in s, to two significant figures.
explanation: Usable energy $= \tfrac{1}{2}C(5.0^2 - 3.0^2) = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 2200 \times 10^{-6} \times 16 = 0.0176\ \text{J}$. Time $= \dfrac{0.0176}{0.020} = 0.88\ \text{s}$. Using $\tfrac{1}{2}C(5.0 - 3.0)^2$ is wrong: subtract energies, not p.d.s.
workedSolution: 1. Usable energy $= \tfrac{1}{2}C(5.0^2 - 3.0^2) = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 2200 \times 10^{-6} \times 16 = 0.0176\ \text{J}$. Time $= \dfrac{0.0176}{0.020} = 0.88\ \text{s}$. Using $\tfrac{1}{2}C(5.0 - 3.0)^2$ is wrong: subtract energies, not p.d.s.
hints: Energy available = energy at 5.0 V − energy at 3.0 V.

stem: When a capacitor is charged from a battery through a resistor, using a resistor of smaller resistance reduces the energy wasted.
explanation: False. A smaller resistance gives a larger current for a shorter time; the energy dissipated is always ½QE, half of that supplied.

stem: Match each pair of known quantities with the most direct formula for the energy stored.
explanation: All three are equivalent via Q = CV; pick the form that uses the given data.

stem: Complete the explanation of the factor ½.

payload.template: As the capacitor charges, the p.d. rises {{blank:a}} from zero to V, so the average p.d. through which the charge is moved is {{blank:b}}. The energy stored is therefore Q × V/2.

explanation: V ∝ Q, so the average p.d. is V/2 and W = ½QV.

stem: What fraction of the energy supplied by a battery is stored in a capacitor that it charges fully through a resistor?
explanation: **Half**: the battery supplies QE and ½QE is stored.

stem: Show that the energy stored in a capacitor of capacitance C charged to p.d. V is ½CV².

points.description: Work done to add charge ΔQ at p.d. V is VΔQ, so energy = area under the V-Q graph.
V ∝ Q (V = Q/C), so the graph is a straight line through the origin and the area is ½QV.
Substituting Q = CV gives W = ½CV².

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Adding charge ΔQ at p.d. V needs work VΔQ, so the energy stored is the area under the graph of V against Q. Since V = Q/C, this is a straight line through the origin, and the area is a triangle, ½QV. With Q = CV, W = ½CV².

explanation: Area under a straight-line V-Q graph.
hints: What does the area under a V-Q graph represent?

stem: Explain why a camera flash uses a capacitor rather than connecting the flash tube directly to its battery.

points.description: The flash needs a very large power for a very short time (about a millisecond).
A battery cannot deliver such a large current/power (its internal resistance limits it).
The battery charges the capacitor slowly; the capacitor then releases its stored energy very quickly through the low-resistance tube, giving the large power.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The flash needs thousands of watts for about a millisecond. A small battery's internal resistance limits it to a few watts, so it charges the capacitor slowly over a second or so; the capacitor can then deliver its stored energy through the flash tube in a very short time, giving the required large power.

explanation: Slow charge, fast release, so a large power.
hints: Compare the power the battery can supply with the power the flash needs.

stem: Explain where the 'missing' half of the energy goes when a battery charges a capacitor, and why the amount lost does not depend on the resistance of the circuit.

points.description: It is dissipated as thermal energy in the resistance of the circuit (wires, internal resistance), with a little radiated.
With a smaller resistance the current is larger but flows for a shorter time (time constant RC is shorter).
These effects cancel: the total energy dissipated (∫I²R dt) is always ½QE.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The energy is converted to thermal energy in the resistance of the circuit, including the battery's internal resistance, with a small amount radiated. Reducing the resistance makes the current larger but shortens the charging time (RC is smaller), and the two effects exactly balance, so the energy dissipated is always ½QE.

explanation: Energy dissipated is independent of R.
hints: What happens to the current and the charging time when R is made smaller?

stem: A defibrillator contains a $40\ \mu\text{F}$ capacitor charged to $3.0\ \text{kV}$. It is discharged through the patient's chest in about $5.0\ \text{ms}$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the charge stored, in C.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the energy stored, in J.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the average power delivered during the discharge, in W, to two significant figures.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: The charging circuit is 75% efficient. Calculate the energy taken from the supply to charge the capacitor, in J.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: A second shock needs 200 J. Calculate the p.d. needed, in kV, to three significant figures.
parts.explanation: $V = \sqrt{2W/C} = \sqrt{400/(40 \times 10^{-6})} = 3.16 \times 10^{3}\ \text{V} = 3.16\ \text{kV}$. Energy ∝ V², so V does not scale linearly with W.
parts.workedSolution: 1. $V = \sqrt{2W/C} = \sqrt{400/(40 \times 10^{-6})} = 3.16 \times 10^{3}\ \text{V} = 3.16\ \text{kV}$. Energy ∝ V², so V does not scale linearly with W.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: State two safety precautions for staff using or servicing a defibrillator.

points.description: Nobody touches the patient (or the bed) during the shock: 'stand clear'.
Discharge the capacitor safely through a resistor before servicing; the kilovolt p.d. can remain after switch-off.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Everyone stands clear of the patient and bed when the shock is delivered, and before servicing the capacitor is discharged through a suitable resistor, because it can hold a lethal charge after the unit is switched off.

explanation: Q = CV, W = ½QV = ½CV²; power = energy/time.

stem: Chipo charges a $680\ \mu\text{F}$ capacitor (tolerance $\pm 10\%$) to $(10.0 \pm 0.1)\ \text{V}$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Describe the graph of p.d. against charge for the charging capacitor and state what its area represents.

points.description: A straight line through the origin with gradient 1/C, ending at (Q, V).
The area under it (a triangle, ½QV) is the energy stored.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: p.d. against charge is a straight line through the origin with gradient 1/C, ending at Q = CV; the triangular area under it, ½QV, is the energy stored.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the energy stored, in J, to two significant figures.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the energy, to two significant figures.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Explain which uncertainty dominates and how the energy could be determined more accurately.

points.description: The 10% tolerance of the capacitance dominates.
Measure C directly (e.g. from a discharge time constant or a coulombmeter) before using it, rather than relying on the marked value.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The ±10% tolerance in C dominates the ±2% from the p.d. The energy would be more accurate if C were measured first, for example from the time constant of a discharge through a known resistor, rather than taken from the marking.

explanation: W = ½CV²; percentage uncertainties add, with V's doubled.
hints: For V², double the percentage uncertainty.
